list.listitem: Destruction of warts, molluscum, or condyloma as therapy.
Destruction of actinic keratoses.
Destruction of benign lesions for cosmetic reasons such as skin tags and seborrheic keratoses.
Decreasing pigmentation in lesions for cosmetic reasons—lentigos, dermatofibromas.

Destruction of basal cell cancers or squamous cell cancer by an experienced practitioner. Consider referral or other treatment options for these patients, and only use liquid nitrogen for cancerous lesions because of its colder temperature.

Cryosurgery is performed by many techniques; the most common are described in stepwise fashion below. The goal is to freeze the contents of the cells to the point at which ice crystals form and cause cell death and tissue destruction. Melanocytes freeze at −5°C, whereas keratinocytes require −50°C. This differential allows a light freeze to be used to depigment lesions, but also explains the potential side effect of hypopigmentation. Studies directly addressing how long and how many times to freeze are sparse, but the Cochrane database lists 4 studies with at least partial data indicating that a more aggressive approach for plantar warts—a double freeze (instead of a single freeze) or a longer time of freeze—results in a 52% success rate compared with a 31% success rate for a conservative approach, but at the risk of a higher frequency of blistering and pain.
Counsel patient regarding treatment options and obtain consent, either verbal or written per local practice.
Fill a spray gun with liquid nitrogen and replace the lid to allow pressure to build up.
Hold the desired tip size of the gun 1 to 2 cm from the lesion.
Depress trigger and freeze the lesion to the desired freeze margin; a pulsing spray technique may be useful to limit diameter of freeze or increase depth of freeze (see ).
Use a zigzag or rotary motion to limit the depth of freeze for superficial lesions (eg, actinic keratoses, lentigos, or flat warts).
Repeat after the lesion has thawed for increased effect as needed.

listitem.strong: Cryosurgery with liquid nitrogen applied with a cotton swab:

list.listitem: Fill a styrofoam cup or insulated container with liquid nitrogen.
Dip a cotton swab into the liquid nitrogen and then apply to the lesion.
Freeze the lesion to the desired freeze margin (see ). This may require redipping and reapplying the swab.
You may wrap additional cotton onto the swab to treat larger lesions or remove or taper the cotton for tiny lesions.
Repeat after the lesion has thawed for increased effect as needed.
Cryosurgery of skin tags with cryotweezers:
Fill a styrofoam cup or insulated container with liquid nitrogen to a depth of 1.5 cm.
Dip a cryotweezers into the liquid nitrogen to chill, approximately 30 seconds and the vigorous bubbling will subside.
Grasp the skin tag (or base of large skin tags) with the cryotweezers and hold until the freeze margin reaches the normal skin at the base of the skin tag.
Allow the skin tag to thaw and then repeat, redipping the cryotweezers as needed.

listitem.strong: Cryosurgery with compressed nitrous oxide or carbon dioxide gun with metal probe:

list.listitem: With desired tip size in place, turn on the gas source and cryogun.
Apply a water-based gel to the tip or the lesion, then touch the tip to the lesion.
Depress the trigger to initiate the freeze and hold in place until the desired freeze margin is achieved (see ).
Repeat after the lesion has thawed.
Clean metal probe tip and turn off gas source.

listitem.strong: Cryosurgery with a mechanically cooled probe:

list.listitem: After the cooling unit has reached at least −75°C remove the probe from the unit.
Place the probe cover on the tip and apply to the lesion.
Freeze the lesion to the desired freeze margin (see ).
Repeat after the lesion has thawed.
Select the appropriately sized cone to completely surround the lesion and a margin of normal skin, and place the tip firmly around the lesion.
Depress the trigger of the spray can and fill the cone to fill line approximately 1/4 inch.
Keep the tip firmly against the lesion until all liquid has evaporated.
Repeat after the lesion has thawed.

listitem.strong: Cryosurgery with direct spray of nitrous oxide:

list.listitem: Activate disposable unit or load cartridge in re-usable unit.
Hold vertically 1 to 2 cm over lesion and activate spray for indicated amount of time based on lesion.
Pitfalls:
Treating lesions of uncertain etiology can lead to treatment failure and undiagnosed cancer.
All wart treatments are subject to a high failure rate (40% or higher).
More aggressive cryosurgery is more effective, but causes more swelling and eschar formation.
Darkly pigmented patients can have very noticeable depigmentation from cryosurgery.
Slow or poor healing can occur in debilitated patients or areas of poor circulation.
Over-the-counter (OTC) cryotherapy devices are widely available for treatment of benign cutaneous lesions, including: Common warts Skin tags (acrochordons) (FDA-cleared since ~2022)

These devices use aerosolized cryogens, less potent than liquid nitrogen typically: Dimethyl ether/propane mixtures Nitrous oxide Deliver freezing via foam or metal applicatorsEfficacy: Clinical effectiveness is lower than liquid nitrogen cryotherapy A randomized trial of a nitrous oxide–based device showed: ~64% complete clearance after ≤3 treatments ~30% resolved after a single treatment ~7% clearance with a comparator device Overall, OTC devices provide moderate but inconsistent clearance
Non-resolving lesions should be evaluated clinically Clinical Role: OTC cryotherapy may be appropriate for: Small skin tags Common warts in accessible locations Patients preferring self-treatment

If the lesion persists, partially resolves, or recurs, re-evaluate the diagnosis, then as appropriate, retreat it with a more aggressive freeze or switch to alternative therapy. (If cancer, consider surgical treatment, radiation therapy, or other options).

Erythema, pain, and swelling are expected, starting from the time of procedure. Blistering is very common and part of the destruction process. It may occur within the first few hours, followed by sloughing or eschar formation in 1 to 3 days. The lesion can be covered with petrolatum ointment with an adhesive bandage to facilitate moist healing. Healing is usually complete within 2 to 3 weeks, may take longer on plantar/thick skin.
Hypopigmentation—may be permanent but can partially or completely resolve after 6 to 12 months.
Blood vessels may rupture leading to large hematoma, which resolves with time.
Neurapraxia tends to resolve with time.
Have the patient call or return to the clinic for reevaluation if complications occur.
Cryotherapy remains one of the most common treatments for warts. However, laser therapy techniques are emerging as an additional therapeutic option in the treatment of nongenital warts.
Repeated treatments may be required for warts that do not resolve or that start to regrow.
Cryosurgery appears no more effective than salicylic acid (SA) for plantar warts.
For cutaneous warts (especially common warts), one RCT found cryosurgery more effective (39% vs 24% for SA vs 16% for wait and see).

In a meta-analysis of local treatments for cutaneous warts, Cochrane authors found no benefit of cryosurgery over placebo or SA for warts at all sites.There was also no difference in cure rates between cryosurgery given at 2-, 3-, and 4-weekly intervals. Aggressive cryosurgery appeared more effective than gentle cryosurgery, but adverse effects were increased. Combined SA and cryosurgery appeared more effective than SA alone (RR 1.24; 95% CI 1.07-1.43).
Duct tape has been of interest in recent years as it is safe and easy to apply. But the above Cochrane review found two studies of almost 200 patients revealing no benefit over placebo.

In a systematic review of treatments for superficial basal cell carcinoma, the tumor-free survival rate for cryosurgery was 67% at 5 years, although data were of limited quality. An evidence-based review of 29 RCTs suggested that surgical excision should remain the gold standard of treatment for basal cell cancer.

In a review of 118 observational studies covering seven treatment modalities for squamous cell carcinoma, the authors found that cryosurgery treatment resulted in the lowest recurrence rate of SCC when the lesion was small and low risk.

For the treatment of actinic keratosis, Cochrane authors concluded that photodynamic therapy was more effective than cryotherapy and had a better cosmetic outcome. A recent meta-analysis to determine relative efficacies of eight standard treatments found that “field directed” therapy (eg, 3% diclofenac in 2.5% hyaluronic acid or 0.5% 5-fluorouracil) outperformed “lesion-directed cryosurgery” in areas of multiple lesions. Remaining lesions can then be treated with cryosurgery or alternative methods.
OTC cryotherapy provides a convenient, but less effective alternative to liquid nitrogen cryotherapy - the most reliable method.

Time off from work is usually not necessary, but cryosurgery for plantar warts can cause pain with walking.
Nurses, physicians, and assistants should be familiar with the instruments, proper cleaning and handling to avoid damage to the instruments or harm to the patients or staff.
